items.title: Very impressed with LFM2.5-24-A2B in Pi Agent
items.excerpt: Just downloaded the new LFm2.5-24B-A2B LiquidAI model for testing. They claimed some pretty good performance, and I've had good experiences with their prior releases. Some context - I use Ornith 1.5-35B pretty regularly in multiple workflows - sometimes on it's own, and sometimes as part of an AI-Council in Pi Agent. It's been very reliable, provides surprising insight "smarter" models miss, and is a great workhorse in Pi. I swapped LFM 24B in to replace Ornith in a few of my workflows - it is holding up REALLY well. It's very fast (~95 tps sustained in llama.cpp using ROCM on an AMD W7900 - latest llama.cpp build). The Q8 takes up 30GB vram with full 128k context. It hasn't failed me yet in my mechanical tasks - it just keeps going and going and going and seems to tick all the boxes for a "little" model I run alongside a larger or smarter model on my other GPU. For "insight" I'll have to test it longer in my council-mode workflow but I will report back. items.summary: Just downloaded the new LFm2.5-24B-A2B LiquidAI model for testing. They claimed some pretty good performance, and I've had good experiences with their prior releases.

items.title: 4x R9700 builds with $127 used EPYCs: $10.7k all-in per machine. I built three (384GB VRAM)
items.excerpt: I saw the 4x R9700 build for a 10-person startup here a few days ago and wanted to share my results, since I opted to spend most of the money on the cards. I went with a super cheap used EPYC instead of a Threadripper. In the end it came to about $10.7k per box all-in, and I built three of them for a total of 384 GB of VRAM. As a long time lurker on my other account, I'm always frustrated that people never show how they actually use the models, so after a lot of back and forth I decided to share the actual project they power instead of being vague. I use these to run the AI behind my business, USA Arms. We organize tens of thousands of firearms-related businesses (gun dealers, ammo dealers, ranges, etc.) and that info is always changing, so we need a system that keeps the site up to date. The models check source facts, sort out business identities, and pull out stuff like services and hours. Every answer gets verified against what the agent actually saw, and we store the documentation so bigger models can audit the work. items.title: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.14005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. items.title: The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.14115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models have significantly lowered the barrier to writing code. Naturally, this has also led to the development of data science agents that promise automating the design and execution of data science from task formulation to model development. Existing evaluations of agentic data science (agentic DS) assess downstream predictive performance and code correctness, providing preliminary insight in agentic DS capabilities. We argue that these evaluations overlook the fundamental principles of data science: methodological data science- and domain knowledge. As such, only assessing downstream performance masks methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation, limiting the development of robust agentic DS systems. In this paper, we evaluate agentic DS beyond accuracy from three different angles: 1) a large-scale analysis of failure modes in common agentic DS frameworks and models across 220 data science tasks, 2) a reusable and extensible test suite with curated data science tasks that test for six specific failures in a controlled manner, and 3) a qualitative assessment of agentic DS pipelines against

items.title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.14118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. items.title: Correction Training for Diffusion Models
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.14136v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Iterative sampling in diffusion models can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. The denoiser is trained on real images interpolated with noise, but at inference its inputs are constructed from its own imperfect predictions from the earlier steps, something it has never seen at training time. This might be one reason diffusion models often struggle without additional help, such as CFG. We introduce a correction step for diffusion models which attempts to reduce this training-inference gap. The corrector takes the base model's prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we iteratively refine the denoiser's clean-sample prediction. This allows us to correct predictions at intermediate denoising steps, preventing early artifacts from persisting into the final sample. items.title: PsyBer-Agent: A Psychology-Driven User Agent for Recommender Systems
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating recommender systems before deployment requires simulators that remain realistic over long, closed-loop interaction cycles. Current LLM-based agents generally function as surface imitators that generate realistic short-term responses but fail to capture the underlying user dynamics such as fatigue, affect, and shifting preferences. We propose PsyBer-Agent, a psychology-inspired simulator that models these dynamics through its Psy-Engine. This engine represents each user with three evolving, model-defined latent states. To calibrate simulated behavior against real interaction logs, we align log-conditioned reference trajectories with simulator-generated latent-state trajectories via Unbalanced Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport. This approach provides structured supervision for a lightweight policy without the computational burden of fine-tuning the backbone LLM. We also introduce WebSim and the PsyBer Benchmark, which encompass multimodal scenarios and seven recommender backbones.
